chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibrahim al-Karkhi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man who had a great town, and in it were Dhimmi dependents. The Sultan would take the Jizyah from them, and he would give them [the collected amount]. From one of them, fifty would be taken, and from some of them, thirty, and less and more. So the owner of the town would make a settlement with the Sultan on their behalf, then he would take from them more than what he gave to the Sultan.
He (peace be upon him) said: 'This is prohibited.'

key_terms.عُلُوجٌ: Dependents or subjects (often used for Dhimmis in this context)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on leasing land from the government and collecting taxes from non-Muslim residents for profit?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi elucidates the permissibility of the 'Iqta' or tax-farming system, where a lessee collects Jizyah from Dhimmi residents and remits a fixed sum to the Sultan. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) declares the practice of retaining the surplus as Haram, reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on preventing exploitation and ensuring that taxation remains a public duty rather than a private profit center. This ruling underscores the ethical dimension of fiscal governance in Islamic jurisprudence, linking economic justice to religious obligation.
